speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, elementary and secondary school pupils spend roughly 1,000 hours per year in the classroom.
Recognizing the importance that the curricula plays in school and in education, parents, students themselves, teachers, public servants and the ministers of education for whom they work have been working extremely hard, and will continue to do so, to remove violence and negative and inappropriate stereotyping from curriculum found in schools.
It has also been noted that these same young people spend roughly the same amount of time watching television. What has been the minister's response to this concern about the impact that violence on television could have on these young people? Well, he has turned it over to the CRTC. That is not a bad first step but I would ask the minister to take a personal initiative here to address this important issue immediately and to bring forth guidelines.

Canadian parents expect the minister to do everything possible to remove violence from television and the media.

Mr. Speaker, July 1 is Canada's birthday. It is also the birthday of one of New Brunswick's and, indeed, Canada's finest citizens.
On July 1 the hon. Cy Sherwood will turn 75. Senator Sherwood has served his country well. Cy was first elected to the New Brunswick legislature in 1952 and was subsequently re-elected in 1956, 1960, 1963, 1967 and 1970. Cy Sherwood served as New Brunswick's Minister of Agriculture from 1952 to 1960, and also served as the Leader of the Opposition and the Leader of the P.C. Party in New Brunswick, from 1960 to 1966.
Cy Sherwood retired, or at least thought he retired, from politics and chose not to run in the 1974 election. However, Cy was appointed to the Senate by the Rt. Hon. Joe Clark on October 3, 1979. Needless to say, Cy Sherwood continued to serve his province and his country with the same level of commitment and integrity that has been the hallmark of his life.
On July 1, 1990, Cy Beverly Sherwood will retire from the Senate of Canada. On behalf of all the members in this House, I wish Senator Sherwood and his wife Madilene a most happy retirement.

Mr. Speaker, last night the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources destroyed one of the few remaining arguments in favour of the Hibernia megaproject-that it would increase Atlantic Canada's energy security. He agreed, during a meeting of the legislative committee on the Hibernia bill, that the government could not even guess what proportion of Hibernia oil would actually be refined in Newfoundland or anywhere else in Canada.

June 13, 1990
In fact, there are indications that most of Eiibernia's oil will How south to the United States, straight off the Hibernia platform. More than $3.5 billion of Canadian taxpayers' money will be placed at risk, including a gift of over $1 billion, which could have gone to the people of Newfoundland and Labrador, but which will instead go to subsidize American energy consumers. This is on top of the inadequate and unsecured employment and industrial development benefits from the project, coupled with the project's negative environmental impacts. A more disgusting illustration of this government's contemptible energy policy is difficult to imagine.

Mr. Speaker, "The world at your door" will be the theme for the Ninth World Folklore Festival in Drummondville, from July 6 to July 16.
Some thirty folk dance groups from five continents will bring you the magic of song, music, dance and folklore of various nations.
Fifteen hundred participants from Canada, the United States, France, Brazil and countries as far away as Israel, Cameroon and Russia, will amaze you with their performances of traditional dances, full of charm, beauty and feeling.
More than 1,800 volunteers are working very hard to make this cultural festival the best ever. Last year, we had 750,000 visitors, and the festival was proclaimed "tourism event of the year" in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I invite all my colleagues and all Canadians to attend this international festival.
The warmth, energy and enthusiasm of the people of Drummondville, together with the spectacular program offered during this ten-day festival, will make your visit unforgettable.

Mr. Speaker, June 25 marks the fortieth anniversary of the beginning of the Korean War.
Between June, 1950, and July, 1953, a total of 26,791 Canadians volunteered their services under the United Nations Charter. Five hundred and sixteen lost their lives and more than 1,000 were wounded. The United Nations intervention in Korea was a move of outstanding historical significance. For the first time, an international organization with a multinational force had intervened effectively to stem aggression.
To date, our Korean veterans have received two medals from the United Nations and the Commonwealth. Their service has yet to be officially recognized by the Canadian government.
It is time that the Canadian government gave recognition to the generosity of spirit that inspired young men and women to risk their lives in the name of peace, freedom and security.
The striking of a distinctive Canadian Volunteer Korean Service Medal would be applauded by all Korean War veterans.
Let us take a moment, on June 25, to remember their great contribution.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ken James (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is National Access Awareness Week, a time to focus national attention on the contributions and concerns of Canadians with disabilities. The spirit engendered by this week is clearly intended to last all year round. Canadians across the country are invited to commit themselves ever more deeply to the full integration of people with disabilities in the life of our society.
This year we are privileged to have the generous sponsorship of nine corporate partners; Bell Canada, Cadillac Fairview Corporation, Canadian National, Esso Petroleum Canada, Ford Motor Company of Canada Ltd., IBM Canada, McDonald's Restaurants of Canada Ltd., Royal Bank and Sears Canada Inc. Each of these
June 13, 1990

corporate sponsors is committed to promotion of employment equity, full and equal access to goods and services for all Canadians and the accurate portrayal of persons with disabilities in advertising and communications.
The active involvement of the private sector at the provincial and local level is fast becoming a tradition during National Access Awareness Week. It clearly reminds us that this week was indeed founded on the principle of partnership among Canadians from every sector of society.
Let us use this occasion to thank this year's corporate sponsors who are promoting the ideals of a barrier-free Canada in every practical way.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today in the House to pay tribute to the dedication of all Canadians who throughout the year help 3.5 million disabled persons in Canada to be participating members of our society.
Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to mention the continuing dedication of agencies and volunteers in my riding, such as the Association de la rose bleue, Les Amis de Repentigny, the Richelieu Club and the Lions Club, to name only a few.
This kind of commitment, which should be an inspiration to us all, receives special attention during National Access Awareness Week, from June 10 to June 16.
The purpose of National Access Awareness Week is to make significant changes in the daily lives of all people who have a disability and to assess the progress achieved during the past year.
And, above all, this week should be an opportunity for reflecting on what remains to be done.

Mr. Speaker, the first nominee for the corporate welfare bum of the week is Trilon Financial. It received a tax credit of $17 million on profits of $218 million in 1988.
The second nominee is Steinberg. In a statement released yesterday the company bragged of how it managed to avoid paying hundreds of millions of dollars in capital gains tax. It used something called a "butterfly" transaction to float away with taxes from the federal treasury. It floats like a butterfly and stings Canadians like a bee.
The third nominee is the Great Lakes Group which paid only $1.9 million on profits of $96 million in 1988.
The envelope, please. And the winner is Trilon Financial. Like many other financial companies, Trilon has benefited from tax breaks that allow holding companies to avoid income taxes. For paper shuffling its way out of paying its fair share, Trilon Financial is the corporate welfare bum of this week.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to talk about the situation in Romania. We heard overnight news reports that the Romanian government has moved into University Square and cleared out the demonstrators.
When I and other members of this House had an opportunity to speak with these demonstrators we found they were not the vagabonds described by president-elect Ion Iliescu but Romanians concerned about their future and concerned about the democratic life they were trying to achieve.
We have just heard from the Secretary of State for External Affairs that he is prepared to allow the Candu project to continue despite the fact there are numerous human rights violations by the Romanian government. The verdict is still out on that government and we call upon the Canadian government to hold a public inquiry to investigate conditions in that country so that we do not end up being responsible for another Chernobyl.

Mr. Speaker, this morning on page 31, the Journal de Montreal published an ad, in very poor taste, in connection with the Saint-Jean holiday in Quebec.

June 13, 1990
Oral Questions
In the ad, readers of the Journal de Montreal are offered a T-shirt which shows a Quebecer walking and tearing up the Canadian flag.
Like many other Quebecers, I cannot condone advertising a T-shirt intended to arouse feelings of hatred and contempt in our two founding peoples. The Canadian flag also belongs to Quebecers.
Mr. Speaker, millions of Quebecers felt humiliated when residents of Brockville, Ontario, trod on the Quebec flag on September 6, 1989.
I am sure that today, most Quebecers will join me and members of this House in condemning this advertisement and asking the Journal de Montreal to withdraw the ad immediately.
Quebec is capable of celebrating its national holiday and parading its flag with respect, dignity and pride.
A Happy Saint-Jean to all Quebecers!

Mr. Speaker, after six years in power, the government is finally listening to Canadians on the environment.
The green paper for public discussion is simplistic and outdated, but it is not discouraging Canadians from participating constructively in large numbers. Their message to the government is this: Act now. The water, air, soil and natural resources need urgent attention. Since the economy is built on the environment, stop treating the two as being separate. Government will be able to protect the environment and promote sustainable development only when departments and agencies adopt such a responsibility.
Canadians have high expectations. Their patience is wearing thin. Their ideas are well ahead of those in government. They are encouraged by the participation of the part-time Minister of the Environment. But does he realize that time is of the essence?
We urge him to meet public expectations by acting expeditiously and by ensuring an environmentally sustainable future for Canadians and the global community.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister in the absence of the Prime Minister.
Since Monday, when the Prime Minister announced the appointment to the Senate of Stan Waters who was elected by the people of Alberta to represent their province in the Senate, the Prime Minister has said that he does not want any more such elected senators for at least five more years.
The Prime Minister can hardly expect Canadians to take him seriously when one day he says he is in favour of an elected Senate, and the next day he says he does not want any more such elected senators for at least five
years.
I ask the Deputy Prime Minister this: Does the Prime Minister have a commitment from all the provinces on this and, if so, exactly what is it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the difference between this government and the government of which the Leader of the Opposition was a member, prior to 1984, is that we are taking Senate reform seriously. That government talked a great line, but did nothing.
As all hon. members know, for the first time in the history of Canada we have laid out an arrangement for comprehensive Senate reform which is based upon the fact that the Senate should be elected. It should have effective powers while retaining and preserving the principle of responsibility of the government to the House of Commons. As well, it should preserve the principle that the Senate would be more equitable in terms of its distribution, so that the less populated areas would have greater participation in the decision-making process in Canada. There is a time-frame that is laid out for that.
I think the hon. Leader of the Opposition should applaud the Prime Minister for clearly demonstrating his commitment to the principle of Senate reform and his clear commitment to the principle of an elected Senate.
June 13, 1990

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will certainly applaud the Deputy Prime Minister for the way he skated around and failed to give any direct answer whatsoever to my question.
Yesterday, speaking in the Alberta Legislature about that province's procedure for electing senators, Premier Don Getty said:
I talked to the Prime Minister about this: Alberta has the legislation
and Alberta will use that legislation whenever it sees fit. There has
been no commitment to do anything else.
Is the Deputy Prime Minister saying today that the Prime Minister will not accept any senators chosen democratically through election by the people of any province, including the province of Alberta, for the next five years? Can he give us a clear and direct answer?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is a pretty hypothetical proposition that the hon. Leader of the Opposition puts forth.
I have the same press report that he has and it points out that Mr. Getty said he would use the Senate selection proposals when he sees fit to do so.
We have here an agreement that has been signed by all First Ministers which outlines a process. Mr. Getty is an honourable man and I suspect that he will honour that process.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like the Deputy Prime Minister to give some explanation. Fie seems to be saying that he and the federal government consider that Premier Getty has given a commitment not to put forward the names of any Senators elected by the people of Alberta during the next five years. Yet, Premier Getty has said in his legislature that he has made no such commitment.
I would like him to explain that contradiction. [Translation]
Furthermore, what justification does the Deputy Prime Minister have for the fact that representatives elected by the people of a province such as Alberta would not be able to sit in the Senate for the next five years?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is absolutely no contradiction.
The Prime Minister and the Premier of Alberta are very major architects in terms of the constitutional reform process that has been ongoing and particularly with respect to the program outlined for Senate reform. It is clearly outlined and I can assure the hon. member, if there are any differences of interpretation, the Prime Minister and the Premier will clearly iron that out.
I should also advise him that today there have been ongoing discussions and there will continue to be ongoing discussions. For the information of the hon. Leader of the Opposition, the Prime Minister called the new senator-elect, Senator Waters, and invited him to the Chamber. We look forward to his participation.
I think that in itself is the clearest recognition and the clearest acknowledgement of Senate reform. Certainly, it is much more progress than was made in the time when the hon. Leader of the Opposition was in government.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National
Revenue.
Further to the ongoing tragedy of this terrible sale by CN Route to Route Canada and Route Canada Enterprises, records show that tax deductions at source were not remitted to Revenue Canada for over a 12-month period. We all know that, if this happened with any other business in Canada, Revenue Canada would have been on its doorstep and confiscated its assets to protect the taxpayers of the country.
I want to know from the Minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, why this particular company was given such special favoured treatment in the payment of trust funds by the employees. Why?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have said before in the House, no such provisions were given to this company by Revenue Canada. Every effort was taken to obtain the funds due

June 13, 1990
Oral Questions
to that department. I can assure the hon. member and the House that the majority of the funds owing to the government of Canada have been recovered.

Mr. Speaker, I direct my supplementary question to the same minister.
Yesterday, we talked about trust funds. I have here a letter dated June 17, 1986, from the then transport minister, which agrees with the sale and advises the President of CN to consider all of the employee rights and to be particularly cautious about the assets to be transferred in the sale.
There was an alleged concern about this transaction prior to June, 1986. There was an obvious lack of concern about the employees after June, 1986.
Will the minister assure the House that the capital assets of the directors of the company who are personally responsible, Messrs Fingold, Cole, and Ruhland, be garnisheed or seized to protect the taxpayers and the employees?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that my hon. colleague raised the alleged letter. This gives me an opportunity to offer to table the letter and put it on the public record.
The first paragraph of the letter which was omitted from the sensationalist article in The Toronto Star says: "You may recall that while concurring with the decision of the CN Board of Directors to sell CN Route-". That is what is left out of the article, and that is what my hon. friend has not referred to. But it is clearly the case that it was CN that decided to sell Route Canada.
As to my hon. friend's question, he knows very well that it is the duty of the bankruptcy proceedings to follow through and decide if things were handled properly. Also as my hon. friend knows, there is an RCMP investigation going forward according to the media. Surely, that is the place for criminal proceedings to commence or for other charges or action to be taken by the Registrar in Bankruptcy through the bankruptcy court proceedings.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister.
So far, the government has not given a precise indication of what is intended to be put before the House as a result of the First Ministers' Conference last week. I want to remind the Deputy Prime Minister that this party cannot be expected to give its full support until we have seen such precise wording.
Can the Deputy Prime Minister confirm that there is still some problem about the wording of the companion constitutional amendment, and whether his government is committed and is prepared to say today that it will ensure that the companion constitutional amendments will come forward as outlined in a communique from the First Ministers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I can confirm that.

Mr. Speaker, that is a short answer. I take it as a commitment of the government, and we will be holding it accountable. Perhaps if we got more short answers which actually came to the point, we might get further in Question Period.
The agreement from last week's First Ministers' Conference states that, in the 1990 Constitutional Conference, the wording of the Canada clause will be considered.
Owing to the exclusion of aboriginal people last weekend from all the talks concerning the Constitution and again seeing aboriginal people standing on the outside, can the Deputy Prime Minister commit on behalf of his government that aboriginal people will be full participants at the table with a voice when the 1990 Constitutional Conference which is going to discuss the Canada clause is held?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am sure the hon. members of the House know that ministers of the government-the Minister of Justice, the minister responsible for intergovernmental affairs and the Minister
June 13, 1990

of Indian Affairs and Northern Development-have met regularly with aboriginal leadership over the past several months leading up to the important and historic discussions of last week.
There were regular consultations with the leadership of the aboriginal peoples involving government officials last week. I, myself, and other ministers will be meeting again tomorrow with the leadership of the four representative national groups in Ottawa.
I can assure the hon. member that these discussions will be ongoing. If the hon. member would refer to the wording of the actual agreement signed last Saturday evening, she would understand that First Ministers' constitutional conferences on aboriginal issues are to be held once every three years. The first is to be held within one year of proclamation, and the representatives of aboriginal people and the territorial governments are to be invited to participate in these conferences.

Mr. Speaker, the answer of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development begs to be like the answer from the Deputy Prime Minister which is short and to the point.
I am not talking about the constitutional conferences that are referred to in the agreement. I am very familiar with the agreement.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister commit on behalf of his government two things: first, that the federal government has a policy of supporting aboriginal people being designated a fundamental characteristic of Canada in the Canada clause and that that is the government' negotiating position; and second, that aboriginal people will be a participant and have a voice at the constitutional conference which discusses the Canada clause?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I am capable of answering the question.
The agreement reached last Saturday evening provides, under clause 4(2), for a process to define and develop language relating to constitutional recognitions. This process will focus on a recognition of the fundamental characteristics of Canada, beginning with the fundamental role of the aboriginal people in the establishment
Oral Questions
and foundation of our country, that of our two founding linguistic groups and our multicultural communities.
The hon. members of the NDP know that aboriginal people will be invited to appear before special hearings to be commenced July 16 by a special committee of the House of Commons in which they will participate. They will have a full and complete role in the development of this language on constitutional recognition.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. We know that the government was actively involved in the transfer and sale of Route Canada and we know from the letter to which the minister referred that the government was to be kept fully apprised of developments.
Would the minister please advise whether the government was aware that Route Canada intended the real estate split?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer once again to the letter which was typed May 26 and dated June 17.
My hon. friend will know full well from the documents which were released through Access to Information that the agreement of purchase and sale was dated April 4, 1986. Any documentation thereafter was to expedite the
sale.
The words that are used in the letter are "the consummation of the sale". Therefore, anything that the government did thereafter was at the request of CN and CN's lawyers in an effort to consummate the sale.
What my hon. friend refers to was not part of what was referred to the government for expedition.

Mr. Speaker, my question was very simple. It was just whether the government was aware of the intended real estate split prior to the deal being concluded. Obviously, the government does not want to answer.
We know the government was actively involved in the transaction and tried to protect itself by putting in a useless good faith clause, purportedly trying to keep the company operating for three years. We know that there

June 13, 1990
Oral Questions
wasn't any good faith in the deal and that Ruhland stripped the company of its assets.
Why would the government not, at the very least, put in an iron clad guarantee for the workers?

Mr. Speaker, this takes me back to a former Liberal cabinet minister who gave all sorts of iron clad guarantees that were not worth the paper they were written on. There is no way you could put in an iron clad guarantee. My hon. friend knows that. A best efforts undertaking is the normal undertaking used in legal transactions. The best efforts of CN were used.
With reference to the question of the real estate split, the government was not involved in the sale in that way. It was involved in any policy matters. Therefore, the answer is no.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister for International Trade, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. The president of Fruehauf Canada has now announced he is closing the Brantford, Ontario, trailer plant because of the free trade deal, high interest rates and deregulation in the trucking industry.
What plans does the minister have to save these 334 jobs, many of which are in my riding?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to say that what my friend said about free trade is wrong. We still have tariffs of 12 per cent. They were at 15 and they are now still at 12 per cent. The problems at Fruehauf have nothing to do with the free trade agreement. There are many factors which are involved, particularly the fact that the competition is very strong in that sector and they have to compete with the United States and many other companies.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration and myself are working veiy closely with all the programs in her department to help those workers.

Mr. Speaker, maybe the minister should talk to the president of
Fruehauf Canada who said yesterday that it was specifically related to the Canada-U.S. free trade deal.
Given the minister's unwillingness to do anything to save these jobs, will the minister at least keep his government's promise of the last election to bring in these special adjustment programs that are supposedly set up to help these workers?
Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Industry, Science
and Technology): Mr. Speaker, I want to repeat again that with tariffs of 12 per cent this problem has nothing to do with the free trade agreement.
Second, there is a bill on the other side of my friend's wall that has been stalled by the Senate for many, many months. If the member wants to do something to help his people he should ask the senators to pass the bill, please.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister, responding on behalf of the Prime Minister. It is a follow-up to a question asked by my leader a few minutes ago on the Canada clause.
As we all know in this House, under the agreement in the communique issued last Saturday there will be participation of aboriginal people during the aboriginal round at the table of the FMC, but can the Deputy Prime Minister give a commitment today that aboriginal people will be participating at the table at the First Ministers' Conference in Vancouver later on this fall when the First Ministers are discussing the Canada clause as it pertains to the aboriginal people in Canada? That is the commitment we want from the Prime Minister.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows that there is a clear process outlined with respect to bringing about a
June 13, 1990

better consensus and understanding with respect to the so-called Canada clause.
As is indicated in the preamble, the Prime Minister and premiers reviewed various drafts which were submitted by the federal government, the Manitoba government, the Saskatchewan government, the Ontario government and the British Columbia government, and it was undertaken that all of these drafts would be submitted to the committee for further consideration.
The hon. member raises an interesting point but it would seem to me that his suggestion might be somewhat premature having regard for the fact that this work will probably be ongoing at that particular time. We will certainly take that suggestion into consideration and obviously I will convey his interest in that regard to the Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, on a supplementary question. Surely the Deputy Prime Minister recognizes that it is up to the Prime Minister to show leadership at this very critical time when aboriginal peoples are feeling a sense of exclusion as a result of the last process that took place.
Does the Deputy Prime Minister not recognize that in view of the fact that an essential component of the Canada clause is the recognition of aboriginal peoples as distinct societies with distinct cultures and languages in this country, it is fundamentally unacceptable for First Ministers to sit around the table and discuss that issue without the participation of aboriginal peoples? Will he not include aboriginal peoples at the table at the First Ministers' Conference in December?

Five days, six days.

Mr. Speaker, the students understood the minister's promise to be to present a bill before the summer recess, whenever that will be.
Oh, oh!

Let's stick to the principal issue. On June 5, the Canadian Federation of Municipalities endorsed a plea by the city of Montreal to ban all semi-automatic combat weapons. The minister knows that the Ruger semi-automatic used to to kill the 14 young women at the University of Montreal could fire up to 50 rounds of ammunition and is in fact used by several police SWAT teams.
Will the minister respond to this serious and reasonable request and make a commitment to ban that type of weapon? Will she put that in the legislation that she tables?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe the hon. member is in fact misquoting the resolution by the Federation of Canadian Municipalities which I think was directed to military and paramilitary type weapons. But those issues will be addressed in the package that I am bringing before the House.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The minister's monetary policy is having a disastrous impact on the economy of Quebec, which is on the verge of a recession, according to Frangois Dupuis, of the Mouve-ment Desjardins. When will the Minister of Finance revise his monetary policy and reduce interest rates?

Mr. Speaker, we review the monetary policy on an ongoing basis. I had a meeting with the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Canada on Monday. I had a meeting with the Governor the previous week. This is something we do on an ongoing basis.
I have made very clear in this House the basis on which we are following monetary policy?. We are concerned
about the inflationary pressures which are undermining the competitive position of our economy. If we do not get these inflationary pressures under control, companies are going to lose business which will cause a loss of jobs on an ongoing basis. It is this that is driving the monetary policy of the Government of Canada.
As soon as we can see some pressure subsidizing, yes, we will see interest rates decline. Until that time, we must continue to follow the policy that we have been following.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is directed to the same minister. In the past twelve months, 51,000 manufacturing jobs were lost in Quebec because of the disastrous policies of the Minister of Finance. When will the minister finally start listening to the Premier of Quebec, the Conseil du patronat, the Quebec Minister of Finance and all economic partners in Quebec who are asking the minister to reduce interest rates before it is too late for Quebec's economy?

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party of Canada, the New Democratic Party of Canada, and the premiers have been calling upon us to reduce interest rates for almost two years now, but consider what would have happened had we taken that advice in the summer of 1988 or even the summer of 1989. We would have had a rip-roaring inflation problem today that would be doing lasting damage to the competitive position of our economy.
Oh, oh.

I hear some disagreement from the members opposite. Let me ask the members opposite to consider the fact that the unit labour costs of Canada at the start of 1989 were increasing at a rate of 4.9 per cent. At the end of 1989 they were increasing at a rate of 6.9 per cent. At the same time unit labour costs in the United States were increasing at 4.9 per cent throughout the year.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport.
The government has consistently been attempting to place itself at arm's length from the decision to sell off CN Route to the private sector. In fact on June 4 the Minister of Transport said: "It was sold on an arm's length transaction with advice coming to the government from CN as to the best offer".
The sentence in the letter which the minister quoted from earlier today, which he did not complete, goes on to say: "The ministerial task force on privatization asked for some additional information on severance provisions and other employment and service considerations and on the value of land to be transferred to the purchaser by virtue of the sale."
If this was only a one-way situation, that CN was only providing advice, why was the Government of Canada, the Minister of Transport of the day, asking for specific information if it was not for the purposes of modifying the sale agreement which although agreed to had not been finalized at that point in time?

Mr. Speaker, as I indicated earlier, the sale agreement was executed on April 4, 1986 and the sale was consummated on December 6, 1986. Between those times it was necessary for the government, in order to complete the sale, to go through certain matters and certain Orders in Council as requested by CN.
I refer my friend back to the letter which says: "while concurring with the decision of the CN board of directors to sell CN Route".
I refer him also to the letter from Canadian National to The Toronto Star dated June 7, 1990, which has been tabled. It says: "CN and no one else decided to sell its subsidiary."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is quite significant that the members of the Liberal Party who were in government for so long in this country prior to 1984 were never able to put in place measures in Atlantic Canada to address the needs that people of Newfoundland and Labrador are experiencing right now.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
On Thursday, March 8, 1990, the hon. member for Skeena rose on a question of privilege to bring to our attention certain actions by the Department of National Defence which in the hon. member's opinion breached his rights and those of all members of the House.
In order to place this matter before the House, the hon. member referred to and quoted extensively from several confidential documents of a sensitive nature. He agreed to provide copies of the documents in reference to the Chair, to the hon. government House leader and to the House leader of the Official Opposition. The recipients of these documents agreed to respect their confidentiality and the Chair undertook to review the documents, to be in contact with the three parties and to return to the House on this matter at an appropriate time. On March 27, 1990, the hon. member for Skeena wrote to the Chair to provide further relevant information. On May 3, 1990, in response to the hon. member for Skeena's inquiry, I reported that discussions on this matter were proceeding.

The Chair is placed in a rather awkward position in a situation such as this. Serious allegations have been
June 13, 1990

made publicly on the floor of the House respecting breaches of members' privileges, yet the documents on which the allegations are based cannot be made public.
The Chair had hoped to reach a negotiated solution to these difficulties and to inform the House of the terms of that solution, but that was not possible. Accordingly, the Chair will attempt to deal with the matter in the customary fashion, bearing in mind, however, the constraints imposed on this case by confidentiality and the sensitive nature of the material under consideration.

It is part of the public record that the hon. member's claim relates to the investigation of a Department of National Defence scientist by the name of Dr. Mendoza, and that the Human Rights Commission of Canada is seized with those aspects of the matter pertaining to the human rights of Dr. Mendoza.
The hon. member for Skeena set out his claim in three points. He indicated first, that the matter involved his rights as an individual member of Parliament because the investigation extended to telephone calls to his office and his Prince Rupert constituency office. In the second and third instances, the hon. member maintained that the rights of all members of the House were affected because documents pertaining to the investigation suggested:
-	that Canadian law be violated-by the Minister of National Defence during Question Period -
And:
-	revealed a view by the Department of National Defence that "the House" should not be advised of the specifics of these investigations.
I should like to deal with these latter two points immediately.
In support of these points, the hon. member for Skeena read into the record, and I refer to Hansard, page 8965, parts of what he termed, "the key document, Department of National Defence file number PSIF 438 558 462, Record of Conversation".
There are four minutes in that particular document and two attachments to it. As the hon. member has already read three of the minutes and one of the attachments into the record, I think it important to record the fourth and final item. It reads as follows:
Speaker's Ruling 4. In the end I suggested to-
At this point, the name of whoever it was the author is suggesting "to" is blanked out. It goes on:
-that we at least wait for the question. The draft responses (not used) are attached.
One of these draft responses was that which was read into the record by the hon. member for Skeena as recorded at page 8966 of Hansard.
In his intervention in the discussion of this question of privilege on March 8 last, the hon. government House leader stated in relation to the "key document" the hon. member for Skeena referred to:
- he seems to have a document which describes potential strategy being worked out by some officials that might be deployed by the Minister of National Defence in terms of dealing with a particular political issue. But as I heard the Hon. Member, as they devise strategy they seem to be saying that unfortunately this strategy would involve violating the law. You are able to conclude from that, if you choose, that they went ahead anyway. If there is evidence to support that I would like to hear it. Or, you can conclude that they have sat down, worked out a strategy and found that unfortunately they could not proceed with it because it violates the law-
Having had the opportunity to thoroughly review and discuss all the documents presented to the Chair, and having reviewed in its entirety "the key document", on which the hon. member for Skeena placed so much reliance in developing his second and third points, the Chair cannot find that a prima facie case of privilege has been made out in this respect and accordingly I must, with respect, dismiss the second and third points of the hon. member's claim.
I should like now to turn to the first point the hon. member for Skeena set out in his claim, that is, that his privilege as an individual member had been breached because the investigation extended to, in his words, "accessing of calls made to my offices". In the evidence that the hon. member put on the record on March 8, 1990, it was clear that:
1)	the Special Investigations Unit of National Defence attempted and apparently succeeded in obtaining the hon. member's phone numbers, both in Ottawa and in his constituency; and,
2)	a search warrant was issued by Judge Leven in Calgary Provincial Court to search Alberta government telephone offices at Calgary for records of long distance

June 13, 1990
Routine Proceedings
phone calls charged to Dr. Mendoza's residence phone. The warrant was executed.

I think the Chair might be permitted to take judicial notice of the fact that the hon. member's telephone numbers are not closely held. In fact, he lists nine telephone numbers, plus two fax numbers and two Zenith numbers on his official letterhead. That being the case, it could hardly be seriously contended that ascertaining the hon. member's telephone numbers involved any type of clandestine operation or any breach of confidentiality or privilege.

As to the search warrant, it would not appear that the execution of the warrant involved any intrusion into, or interference with, the office or records of the hon. member. It would appear that the investigators simply obtained the telephone numbers of the hon. member which are public knowledge and attempted to match these with the legally obtained record of long distance calls made from Dr. Mendoza's residence. The only information which could be thus obtained was whether or not a call had been placed to the hon. member's office.
As the Chair understands the matter, neither the identity of the parties to any calls, nor the nature or content of any calls would be thus revealed. In these circumstances, the Chair cannot conclude that the hon. member's privileges have been interfered with and accordingly, cannot conclude that a prima facie case of privilege has been made out.
It may be that the hon. member wishes to challenge the information upon which the search warrant was based. In that case, there is a mechanism in the court system for do doing. The Judiciary and Parliament are carefully segregated under our constitution and this House and, in particular, the Chair, cannot sit in review or appeal of the decisions of any court in the land.
In concluding his remarks on this issue on March 8, the hon. member for Skeena said: "When one takes the time to look at the documents that I now have, in sum, one can see that there is something going on that is violating the rights of the members of this House".

The Chair wants to assure the hon. member that the Chair takes this matter very seriously indeed. The Chair has listened with great care to the hon. member, has exhaustively reviewed the documents presented by the hon. member and held discussions with representatives of all parties on this issue prior to deciding that no prima facie case of privilege has been made out in this instance.

It may be that the hon. member could, by the presentation of a cogent argument supported by evidence of true probative value, establish a prima facie case of privilege based on the pattern of events at issue here. The Chair does not preclude that possibility. In deciding as I have, the Chair only signals that such a case has not been successfully made and accordingly, the matter cannot be afforded privileged treatment. In referring to the hon. member's comments of the case, in sum, I repeat, the Chair has taken very serious consideration of the entire situation.
I thank all hon. members for their co-operation and patience in respect of this important matter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour of presenting Bill C-67, the plant protection act, which proposes amendments to the Plant Quarantine Act.
It has been 80 years since the first formal pest control and eradication act was passed in Canada. Over time, a number of adjustments have been made to deal with emerging issues affecting our plant-based industries.
In 1952, for example, Canada responded to growing international concern over the spreading of pests by signing the International Plant Protection Convention.
In 1968, the Plant Quarantine Act was introduced. Over time, however, it became apparent that this legislation required amending because of changes in the world market-place.
In 1982, Agriculture Canada set out to assess the effects of market-place changes, new technology and current legislation on our programs. This has been a time consuming and demanding process and I am pleased to confirm that the results of this review have been well worth the effort. In fact, the legislation before the House today represents a major step in ensuring the continued viability and strength of Canada's plant-based industries.
We anticipate benefits from this legislation in three areas.
First, the act will serve as a demonstration of Canada's commitment to prevent the spread of plant pests that have economic importance to our global trading partners. The net result will be improved opportunities for marketing Canadian plants and plant products and other things internationally.
Second, the new legislation provides for recovery of the costs of program delivery from those who directly benefit from some activities administered under the act. For example, we will be able to recover costs for conducting inspections and issuing permits and other documents to those who import or export plants and

June 13, 1990
Government Orders
plant products. Fumigation, treatment and quarantine of such items will also be cost-recoverable.
A third important thrust of this legislation is to reduce the threat of introducing or spreading a plant pest within Canada. The value of our Canadian plant-based industries is simply too great to risk the significant loss and damage that can be caused by pest infestations.
Having outlined the main objectives behind the new Plant Protection Act, I would like to focus on some of the specific provisions.
A particularly important aspect of this bill is the increased authority it grants to Agriculture Canada inspectors to do their job more effectively. For example, these provisions grant authority to the department to issue permits to persons importing material; to designate where and under what conditions an imported item or an item for export will be inspected; to order the removal, treatment, quarantine, or disposition of items found to be in contravention of the act; and to stop or enter vehicles, ships, rail cars, and other conveyances for the purposes of enforcing the act.
In addition, the responsibility to prove that individuals deliberately spread plant pests will no longer rest solely with the department. In the past individuals have challenged the department to prove such deliberate intent. This has proved to be a serious hindrance to the government's efforts to keep plant pests from entering or spreading within Canada.
The new act has sufficient flexibility to allow for the control or eradication of plant pests without creating undue interference to the transportation and marketing of agricultural and forestry products.
Other amendments update and simplify legal requirements. The penalties for contravening the act have been restructured to make them more effective. New penalties include ticketing for minor offences. This provision will eliminate the need to go through lengthy and expensive courtroom proceedings to prosecute those who plead guilty to such infractions.
Yet another important area addressed in this legislation concerns compensation. Bill C-67 clarifies the conditions when the department will pay compensation and how people can appeal compensation claims.
While we have focused on finding ways to control or eradicate plant pests in Canada, we have also made provisions to keep plant pests from ever reaching our shores in the first place.
Two sections of the act touch on this problem. First, in those cases where the department has reasonable grounds to believe that goods destined for Canada may be infested, officials will be authorized to carry out inspection at the place of origin prior to shipment.
Second, we are interested in working with other companies to help them improve their plant pest control and eradication systems. This act authorizes the department to provide financial aid and technical expertise to foreign countries.
In view of safeguarding our industries, the act also allows material to be detained for longer than the current 90 days. This will be increased to 180 days or longer.
Two new sections of the act provide the Minister of Agriculture with the authority to require operators of land, air, rail and sea terminals to allocate, if required, at no cost to the Crown, space and facilities for the services provided for the proper administration of the act.
Procedures and responsibilities of the department have also been clarified. The process of declaring places to be infested and the powers of the minister and inspectors in this action have been carefully spelled out. The process and authority to prohibit or regulate the introduction or movement of plants, plant products or other things, are also more clearly explained.
We have made every effort to take into account the legitimate and practical concerns of those people who are affected by the decisions taken by inspectors.
Provincial governments, appropriate federal departments, industry, and other interested groups have all had a chance to study and respond to this proposed legislation.
I am very pleased to note that all of those whose efforts contributed to the new act agree that the amendments are necessary and support the principles of the bill.
Our plant based industries rely heavily on our plant protection programs. Their future depends on the improvements and changes found in Bill C-67. For them it will mean improved protection against the spread of plant pests, greater confidence on the part of domestic
June 13, 1990

consumers, and more opportunities for access to foreign markets.
I trust that all members of this House will consider these benefits and give strong support to this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say only a couple of words on the third reading stage of Bill C-67.
This is a highly technical bill, one which perhaps does not catch much notice of members in the House of Commons. However it is very important to our agricultural industry because it has to do with the control of plant diseases and protection from pests. This is very important in a day and age when we have large cargo and passenger planes carrying hundreds of passengers into and out of airports in this country and ships plying the oceans.
This bill expands the existing legislation from about 8 pages of legalise to some 25 pages. I do not say that that it is necessarily good to increase the amount of verbiage in a bill or in an act, but in this case I believe it is.
As we might expect it provides for cost recovery. This government has a penchant for demanding more and more fees from Canadians, as the Minister of Finance has done in every budget since he has become the Minister of Finance on September 19, 1984.
We have tried to get specific details from the government at report stage and in committee, but we have not received a great deal of specifics with regard to the cost recovery. We do believe that certain types of economic activity by groups and individuals where they incur costs for their own benefit are justifiable, whereas where plant diseases inadvertently occur we believe the government has the full responsibility to pay for those costs.
This bill puts an onus on highly technically trained people and researchers to notify the government when they become aware of important diseases from other countries that would have an adverse impact on our agricultural industry. I am not sure the existing legislation puts that onus on people who have the skills to identify foreign pests which could have an adverse
Government Orders
economic impact on our country, but this bill provides for that.
It gives more authority for inspectors to take samples and to identify them for legal activity and prosecutions. That is necessary in this realm of protection of plants in this country.
It provides more flexibility for hiring specialists on a part-time or casual basis who are fully qualified to act as agents of the Crown. That is wise, because in a day and age when we are concerned about costs to the government it is probably better to hire a highly skilled and trained person rather than have to move people all over the country for specific problems that occur.
It provides for compensation to owners of crops that are damaged by pests and infectious agents where it is in the best interests of the nation to pay compensation.
It also provides for the location of inspection stations abroad, for instance, where we are importing plants which could be harbingers or vectors for infectious agents. The example given in the committee hearings was bulbs which are brought into Canada from Holland. It is to ensure that those plant products are investigated and inspected abroad so that we do not run the danger of introducing infectious agents into the country.
There are new offences provisions in the act for higher fines and for ticketing. All of us are familiar with the experience of signing a customs declaration where we state that we have brought no plant or plant product into the country. This will provide for a ticketing system where someone illegally imports plants which may be carrying infectious diseases or pests that could endanger our livestock or our plant industries.
The fact that a ticket can be provided rather than a conviction or charges being laid may be beneficial in making people realize just how important and serious the dangers are to our industry from bringing in plants which are not properly inspected or authorized.
In summary, this is quite a technical piece of legislation. It brings the act up to date. It provides for the changing world in which we live where there is greater transportation, a greater flow of people, products and materials between countries, not only between Canada and the United States but other countries around the

June 13, 1990
Government Orders
world. It generally provides for the protection of the Canadian agricultural industry which is so important to the economy of the country.
We support this bill at third reading and want to see it ultimately implemented by the Government of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak briefly on Bill C-67 to amend the Plant Quarantine Act so as to protect plant life in the agricultural and forestry sectors of the Canadian economy. This is a revision of old acts in an attempt to bring procedures up to date.
There are few questions that some observers may have about the bill. For instance, it grants the authority to operate an import permit system which is absolutely necessary if our country is to control the importation of pests with plants or with parts of plants, including diseases and fungi that might come in with seed.
Something that we will have to wait for and watch is whether this import permit system operated by Agriculture Canada will become noticeable. If and when we ever get to an import basis on American wheat under the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, External Affairs will take over the issuing of those permits for the granting of import licences.
However, we presume that Agriculture Canada will still be required to make certain that those imported seeds and grains are free of disease so that international trade does not override the need for the maintenance of a healthy lifestyle on both sides of the border of the trading countries. This will also keep available Canada's reputation as a country, which is relatively free of plant diseases and plant pests, to utilize in international trade for our own grain trade.
The changes to the act spell out some of the powers that the Department of Agriculture will have. It will be able to stop and enter conveyances whether vehicles, ships, or rail cars for purposes of enforcing the act and to make the inspections that are required to determine whether there are plant products on board and whether those plant products contain diseases or pests. It clarifies that the importer of all items governed by the act is responsible for presenting those items for inspection. It
sets out that there must be rooms and space made available for those inspections to take place.
It is quite a flexible act in that it covers a wide variety of plant material. Changes down the road can be reacted to, it is spelled out in the bill, by changes in regulations at that time. This is basically permissive legislation.
Understanding fully how the new rules will apply is virtually impossible until we see the regulations. Because this type of act has been in place in this country for close to a century we in the opposition parties are prepared to take the department's assurances at face value that these regulations will continue to carry out the functions that the Department of Agriculture has carried out in the past, that it will continue to act responsibly in the future and that regulations will in fact protect producers, consumers and the general health of the population as far as domestic use is concerned, and for the continuation of our good reputation in trading relations.
I am prepared to let the bill have speedy passage and will close my remarks so that that can happen.

There is one motion set down on the Order Paper for the report stage of Bill C-66, an act respecting diseases and toxic substances that may affect animals or that may be trans-

mitted by animals to persons, and respecting the protection of animals. That motion is in order.

Motion No. 1
That Bill C-66 be amended in Clause 64 by striking out line 3 at
page 29 and substituting the following therefor:
"(i) requiring animals to be treated in such a manner as to avoid or minimize the infliction of pain, suffering or injury on or to animals".
He said: Mr. Speaker, I will be quite brief. During the course of the committee hearings on this piece of legislation we heard from quite a broad range of people who are involved in the animal industry in this country as producers, consumers, handlers and processors.
One of the suggestions that came from the Canadian Federation of Humane Societies was that while it had no particular criticism of the bill it would feel better if there were a better description of humane treatment of animals. It suggested a definition something like this which we have translated into parliamentary language which would lay the ground work and the rules for all future regulations concerning the treatment of animals.
As you read, Mr. Speaker, it simply states that it would require animals to be treated in such a manner as to avoid or minimize the infliction of pain, suffering or injury on or to animals. I think this permits Parliament to put in place the ground rules for the humane treatment of animals. I presume that we would have no great discussion on this, that it seems to be reasonable and acceptable and therefore could be passed forthwith.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would just like to point out two or three items.
The present wording of the legislation covers the governing, care, handling and disposition of animals. These words have been chosen because they are used in the title of the recommended codes of practice for the care and handling of animals.
The department has provided funds for the development and publishing of the codes. The codes have been developed for poultry, swine, ranched mink and foxes, veal calves, dairy cattle, and so on.
Government Orders
The development of the codes is co-ordinated by the Canadian Federation of Humane Societies. Representatives from industry groups such as producers, truckers and slaughter plants all have input into those codes.
Professional organizations such as the Canadian Veterinary Medical Association, the Canadian Society of Animal Science and the American Society of Agricultural Engineers provide the expertise in the development of the codes.
The wording of the paragraph proposed by the member for Mackenzie, while interesting, would appear to limit the section to areas where pain, suffering or injury could be inflicted on animals.
I believe that the current wording gives the clause a broader mandate, without the necessity of proving the possibility of pain, suffering or injury.
In addition, the concept of minimizing pain, suffering or injury could be difficult to interpret and might limit the regulations that could be made under this enabling clause.
I would also like to point out that words such as those proposed by the member can be put in the regulations that are prepared under this act. For instance, the current regulations which are made under the Animal Disease and Protection Act use the words "likely to cause injury or undue suffering" to tell people what standards must be met in transporting animals.
These words are more appropriate because they have been tried and tested in prosecutions under the current act and are therefore understood by the industry and Agriculture Canada inspectors.
By putting such words in the regulations rather than in the act each area can be addressed using appropriate words for the specific concern.
We do not believe that the amendment would help the present legislation and could cause us some problems in some ways.

Mr. Speaker, during the course of the debate in the legislative committee on Bill C-66 we had a number of groups, such as the dairy and hog producers, who outlined to us their code of practice for the maintenance of various livestock groups.
